prompt:
Patient is a 45 year old man who lives alone in a suburban apartment with no pets and recently returned from a trip to South America where he was assisting with surgical procedures. One week ago during the trip, after removing his gloves, he noted blood on his finger without a clear tear in his glove or puncture wound. He is HBsAB positive. What is the timing for testing for infectious diseases due to potential exposure?

Provide a comprehensive management plan including appropriate diagnostic workup, referrals, procedures if indicated, follow-up, and actions to avoid.

rubric_items.text: Clarify and document whether blood contacted intact skin, nonintact skin, a mucous membrane, or a percutaneous injury.
Obtain a baseline HIV-1/2 fourth-generation antigen/antibody test now.
Obtain baseline hepatitis C antibody testing with reflex HCV RNA if reactive.
Obtain baseline hepatic function testing, including ALT and AST.
Review hepatitis B vaccination and documented immune-response records; obtain quantitative anti-HBs only if a protective response is not adequately documented.
Arrange source-patient testing for HIV, HBsAg, and HCV RNA when the source can be identified.
Document and report the incident through occupational health.
Refer the patient to occupational health or an infectious disease clinician for exposure management.
If interim HIV testing is indicated, obtain laboratory-based fourth-generation HIV antigen/antibody testing and HIV NAT at 4–6 weeks after exposure.
Obtain final laboratory-based fourth-generation HIV antigen/antibody testing and an HIV nucleic acid test at 12 weeks after exposure.
Obtain HCV RNA at 3 to 6 weeks after exposure.
Repeat HCV antibody testing at 4 to 6 months, with reflex HCV RNA if reactive.
Repeat hepatic function testing if baseline results are abnormal, symptoms suggest hepatitis, or follow-up identifies HCV infection.
Withhold hepatitis B post-exposure prophylaxis if the documented anti-HBs level is at least 10 mIU/mL.
Explain that initiating HIV post-exposure prophylaxis now is not recommended because more than 72 hours have elapsed.
If HIV PEP was already appropriately started within 72 hours, complete 28 days unless subsequent source testing or exposure assessment establishes that PEP is unnecessary.
Counsel the patient to seek prompt evaluation for symptoms of acute retroviral syndrome or acute hepatitis.
For a qualifying potential HIV exposure, recommend barrier protection during sexual activity until final HIV follow-up testing is complete.
Advise the patient to defer blood, tissue, organ, and semen donation until follow-up testing is complete.

For a clinician with a completed vaccine series but no documented prior protective response and current anti-HBs below 10 mIU/mL, revaccinate per CDC guidance and give HBIG when indicated by source HBsAg status; do not boost documented prior responders solely because titers have waned.
Schedule a follow-up visit at approximately 4 to 6 weeks after exposure.
Initiate HIV post-exposure prophylaxis now despite presentation more than 72 hours after exposure.
Administer hepatitis B immune globulin despite documented protective hepatitis B immunity.
Administer a hepatitis B vaccine booster despite a documented anti-HBs level of at least 10 mIU/mL.
Counsel that a single negative baseline HIV test excludes subsequent seroconversion.
Defer all baseline infectious disease testing until six months after exposure.
Obtain only a single HIV antibody test at six weeks without baseline or later follow-up testing.
Order routine baseline HIV RNA testing in place of standard fourth-generation screening.
Use HCV antibody alone at six weeks instead of recommended early HCV RNA testing.
Prescribe empiric direct-acting antiviral therapy for hepatitis C without evidence of infection.
Conclude that no exposure assessment or bloodborne-pathogen testing is needed solely because no puncture wound was seen.
Use serial anti-HBs titers to monitor for hepatitis B transmission.
Order a broad tropical disease serology panel solely because of travel to South America.
Order a malaria blood smear for this asymptomatic blood exposure.
Order routine syphilis, gonorrhea, chlamydia, and trichomonas testing solely for this occupational exposure.
Perform surgical exploration or debridement of the finger without evidence of a retained foreign body or infection.
Prescribe empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics for the finger without signs of bacterial infection.
Instruct the patient to donate blood as a means of determining whether infection occurred.
Forgo exposure-specific prophylaxis and serial follow-up testing if assessment confirms that blood contacted only intact skin.
